title: California Steps Back From Dangerous Expansion of Its Age-Gating Law
summary: California's legislature has, according to the Electronic Frontier Foundation, agreed to strip A.B. 1856 of language that would have pushed age-verification signal collection out to web browsers and individual websites. The EFF, which formally opposed the bill, withdrew that opposition after Assemblymember Buffy Wicks's office reportedly agreed to remove the expansion. The formal text has not yet been updated — the bill's most recent amendment, dated July 1, still lists browser providers and internet website operators as required signal recipients.
body:
When California passed A.B. 1043 last October, it established a specific architecture for age-gating: operating systems would collect a user's age bracket and pass it to covered application stores, which would pass it along to app developers. The Digital Age Assurance Act does not take effect until January 2027. On its face, it does not require websites to verify ages.

A.B. 1856 would have broken that boundary.

The bill, authored by Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, would have extended the signal chain to browser providers and internet website operators. Under the proposed framework, operating systems would have been required to transmit age-bracket signals not just to the App Store or Google Play, but to every browser installed on a device — and through those browsers, to every website that opted in to receive them. Where A.B. 1043 compresses verification into the OS layer, the expansion would have distributed it across the open web.

The Electronic Frontier Foundation filed formal opposition to A.B. 1856 in May 2026. On July 15, the organization reported that the Legislature had agreed to remove the browser and website language, and EFF withdrew its opposition.

"We still believe the law passed last year threatens online anonymity, privacy, and security," EFF wrote — but added that the amendments had addressed the bill's most pressing new harms.

The concession matters, but it has not yet been formalized. The most recent amendment to A.B. 1856, dated July 1, still includes "(C) A browser provider" and "(D) An internet website operator" as required signal recipients under the bill's signal-transmission framework. The bill is currently pending before the Senate Appropriations Committee. No amendment has been filed since July 1. EFF is describing an agreement reached with the bill's author, not a change that has appeared in enacted text.

The distinction is procedural but not trivial. Until the Senate Appropriations Committee or a floor amendment formally strikes those clauses, the expansion EFF describes as abandoned remains in the operative draft.

This is not the first concession California has made during A.B. 1856's passage. In May, after sustained pushback from the open-source community over conflicts with GNU/Linux and other non-commercial systems, the Legislature carved open-source operating systems out of the compliance framework. That change was reflected in the bill text. The browser and website carve-out has not been — yet.

The underlying law, A.B. 1043, remains intact and on schedule. EFF's longstanding position is that even the narrower framework creates conditions that push services toward mandatory age verification: more identity checks, more biometric scanning, more data collected, more data to breach. The July walk-back, if enacted, removes what EFF called the most dangerous extension of that architecture. What remains is still a fundamental change to how Californians — and the services they use — interact with the web.
ai_monologue: The walk-back EFF describes is real — the agreement appears to have been reached — but the bill text hasn't caught up. The sentence that matters isn't written yet.

I wrote accordingly: attribute the step-back to EFF's reporting of what the Legislature has agreed to, note the operative text hasn't been updated, and flag what to check before the article is upgraded to confirmed.
